pattern_findings: Established cards (EOIR, Open Payments, FEC) open with a one-paragraph purpose statement and a bold headline count, then a Quick Start that attaches the public Hugging Face URL with a fixed catalog alias (eoir, op, fec). The three new cards open with pre-publication status prose, and their only runnable Python example opens a local path under releases/, which a Hugging Face reader cannot run.

Hugging Face YAML must be the first bytes of README.md. onet/README.md places a blockquote publication note above the frontmatter, and qcew/README.md and fars/README.md carry no frontmatter at all, so license, pretty_name, tags and size_categories are not parsed on the dataset page. Every established card has valid frontmatter at the top.

Established cards present a Tables section as a Markdown table with per-table rows (Open Payments also gives column counts and coverage). The new cards have row tables but mix grain, key and column counts into free text; dataset-facts.json supplies exact row and column counts for all 22 tables and should be the single source.

EOIR and Open Payments ship an explicit 'Researcher caveats' block as a short numbered list that a reader can scan before publishing numbers. The new cards contain the same substance (suppression flags, non-one-to-one SOC, person-join hazards, BAC 940, omitted MI files) but as dense paragraphs under headings like 'Interpretation and joins' and 'Safe comparisons'.

Established cards end with a concise dated Changelog that states what changed and the resulting counts. The new cards have no changelog; their last sections are rebuild and supervisor detail (memory caps, partial-file handling, guard receipts) that belongs in the source repository, not the researcher-facing card.

Established cards give a GitHub link, the data source with its update cadence, and a one-line license statement separating build code (MIT) from data terms. The new cards state license terms carefully (CC BY 4.0, BLS public domain, NHTSA own policy) but bury them below several screens of audit text and do not link a source repository or dictionary from a navigation block.

No reference card distinguishes R client versions, because the R package did not need it. For these three datasets the supplied consumer evidence shows CRAN datapond 0.1.0 and a patched 0.1.1 behave differently with DuckDB configuration, and neither resolves these ids until the registry entries merge, so the cards must offer a direct DBI/duckdb R example now and label package examples as post-integration.

Open Payments and FEC cards mention the datapond package only as an alternative to direct ATTACH. For these three the registry PRs are draft, so a card that says datapond.connect('onet') works would be false today; the correct pattern is direct URL first, package second with its precondition stated.

The source READMEs for the new datasets are currently identical in purpose to the HF cards, whereas EOIR and Open Payments keep two documents: a researcher card on HF and a builder-oriented README on GitHub with Quick start, Researcher caveats, Remote access, Usage, Tables, Views, Known issues, Data validation. The new source READMEs lack a table of contents and the 'Reproduce and validate' sections run 8 to 12 paragraphs without subheadings.

Artifact identity (bytes, SHA-256, dataset commit) is stated in the new FARS card but not in a consistent place across the three. Established practice (FEC) is one line near the end; the pinned-commit resolve URL is the practical reproducibility hook and should appear next to the main URL in Quick Start.

source_readme_plan.goal: Make each source README read like eoir-source.md and openpayments-source.md: a researcher can find purpose, quick start, tables, views, caveats and license in the first two screens, while every operational and audit sentence is retained verbatim in linked documents.
source_readme_plan.preservation_rule: No sentence is deleted. Paragraphs that move are cut and pasted unchanged into the target file, and the README keeps a one-line pointer with the target's heading. Counts, hashes, dates and limits are not retyped by hand; they are moved as text.
source_readme_plan.frontmatter_rule: Hugging Face copies must start with the YAML block. Move the 'Published October 18, 2026' blockquote below the H1 as a normal paragraph linking PUBLICATION.md. The GitHub source README needs no YAML.
target_structure: H1 title, one-paragraph purpose, bold headline counts, link to the Hugging Face dataset and PUBLICATION.md
Table of contents (links to the sections below)
Quick start: direct DuckDB ATTACH (CLI, Python, R), then the datapond package block labelled 'after catalog integration'
Tables (rows and columns from dataset-facts.json), keys and grain
Researcher caveats as a numbered list (same substance as the HF card, may be longer)
Example queries (link to examples.sql; keep the current inline examples)
Data source, version and provenance summary (ZIP bytes/hash, acquisition date, release vintage) with a link to source-lock.json
Build from source: the three or four command lines only, with a link to docs/REPRODUCE.md
Validation summary: three sentences and a link to docs/VALIDATION.md and the evidence folder
Update procedure: short list, link to docs/UPDATE.md
Status: publication date, artifact hash, registry PR state

source_readme_plan.catalog_dependency: The website cards and headline stats are rendered from registry.json on the registry main branch, which has 16 entries. The three datasets are published on Hugging Face and queryable by URL, but they do not appear on the site, and datapond.connect / dp_connect do not resolve their ids, until the three draft registry PRs are reviewed and merged by the parent. Documentation must say exactly that, link the Hugging Face pages directly, and must not point clients at a self-hosted registry as if it were official. The R consumer test used options(datapond.registry_url=...) only as a localhost harness; it is not offered as a user instruction.
source_readme_plan.link_integrity: Before publishing, confirm the GitHub repository names, that DICTIONARY.md and examples.sql exist at the linked paths on main, that the Hugging Face artifact filenames are onet.duckdb and qcew.duckdb, and that PUBLICATION.md states the dataset commit shown in dataset-facts.json.

website_changes.change: Replace with: var sizeDisplay = (db.size_gb == null) ? '--' : (db.size_gb < 1 ? Math.round(db.size_gb * 1000) + ' MB' : (Math.round(db.size_gb * 10) / 10) + ' GB');
website_changes.why: size_gb is bytes/1e9 (registry entries use 0.026489 for 26,488,832 bytes), but the code multiplies by 1024 and only below 0.1 GB. O*NET would show 12 MB instead of 11 MB, FARS 27 MB instead of 26 MB, and QCEW would print the raw decimal '0.195571712 GB' instead of '196 MB'. Existing larger databases keep one decimal in GB.

R direct examples call dbExecute twice for INSTALL and LOAD rather than one multi-statement string; confirm the duckdb R client accepts them and that ATTACH with (READ_ONLY) works over HTTP in the tested DuckDB 1.5.5 R build.
Python examples pass two statements in one con.sql string, matching the EOIR card; confirm against DuckDB 1.5.4 and 1.5.5 Python.

QCEW size_categories uses 1M<n<10M for 3,096,467 rows; HF license: other requires license_name, which is set. Validate the three YAML blocks with the Hub card validator after moving them to the top of each file.

All SQL in the cards reuses examples.sql column names with a catalog alias prefix; Codex should execute each against the public artifacts and confirm the alias-qualified view names (onet.v_skills, qcew.annual, fars.crashes) resolve and that GROUP BY ALL is accepted in the tested DuckDB versions.

The announcement says 'verified at its public URL with HTTP range requests from Python and R'; this relies on the user's statement that public immutable-byte, range, Python and R tests passed, which is not in the supplied evidence files. Keep only if PUBLICATION.md records it.
